questions.stem: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the temperature of the surroundings?
questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction, energy is transferred from the reaction to the surroundings as heat. This causes the temperature of the surroundings to increase.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT typically an exothermic process?
questions.explanation: Thermal decomposition is an endothermic process because energy must be supplied (as heat) to break down the compound. Combustion, neutralisation, and respiration are all common examples of exothermic reactions.

questions.stem: On an energy level diagram for an exothermic reaction, where are the products shown relative to the reactants?

options.text: At the same energy level as the reactants
Energy level diagrams do not show product energy
At a higher energy level than the reactants
At a lower energy level than the reactants

questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction, the products have less energy than the reactants. The difference in energy has been released to the surroundings. On the diagram, the products line is drawn lower than the reactants line.

questions.stem: Which practical application uses an exothermic reaction?
questions.explanation: Self-heating cans use an exothermic reaction (such as calcium oxide reacting with water) to generate heat and warm the contents. Cold packs use endothermic reactions. Photosynthesis is endothermic.

questions.stem: Why is combustion classified as an exothermic reaction?

options.text: Because it releases heat and light energy to the surroundings
Because it always involves carbon compounds

questions.explanation: Combustion is exothermic because it releases energy (heat and often light) to the surroundings. The energy released when new bonds form in the products is greater than the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants.

questions.stem: What is the sign of the enthalpy change (ΔH) for an exothermic reaction?

options.text: It varies depending on the reaction

questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions have a negative enthalpy change (ΔH < 0) because the system loses energy to the surroundings. The products have less energy than the reactants, so the overall change is negative.

questions.stem: When an acid is added to an alkali in a neutralisation reaction, what would a thermometer in the solution show?
questions.explanation: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction. When acid reacts with alkali, energy is released to the surroundings as heat, so the thermometer would show a temperature increase in the solution.
